top.line: Free to copy, paid at the source: per-use charging for open policies and hooks.
top.para: This newsroom already charges per use from prepaid credit. Our policies and hooks are open, but a hook is code running with your permissions, and a company will not take it from an unknown site. So the official site can charge per use, even for open content. To earn that trust, others review what we publish, and we sign it.

in-short.line: Seven points: per use, open, code, the source, the charge, review, the price.
in-short.para: We already charge per use. Our policies and hooks are open, but a hook is code running with your permissions, so the source matters. The official site can charge per use even for open content, say £1 a page from £50 of credit. To earn it, others must review it, and we sign it. The price is to discover.

meter.para: Every reader starts with £5 of credit; a new article read to the end costs 10p, an older one 5p, other pages less. Readers can set a page's price from free to double, the balance can go below zero, and a £5 top-up link has been live since 11 October. The book's website runs the same meter.

open.line: Open, and still worth coming to the source.
open.para: The vocabulary and policies are CC BY 4.0 and the code Apache 2.0. But some policies are code: Claude Code says a plugin can execute arbitrary code with your privileges and hooks run with full user permissions. A copy of a hook from an unknown site is like software from an unknown source, so companies come to the official site.

charge.para: Even under an open licence, use of the official site can be metered: £1 for a page with a reviewed hook, drawn from £50 of credit, or much less; the price is to discover with our first customers. Running and copying a hook stay free; the visit to the source is metered. Red Hat and Docker show companies already pay for this.

review.line: Not trust us: reviews and audits by others.
review.para: Policies and hooks should be reviewed by others and the record published beside them. Services exist: Cisco's Skill Scanner, Snyk's Agent Scan, NVIDIA's SkillSpector, NeMo Guardrails and garak, Socket's audits, Anthropic's scanned community marketplace. No scanner is enough: one rated a lethal-trifecta skill SAFE. So the record holds both scans and a named human sign-off.

signed.line: Signed, so the source can be checked.
signed.para: Every policy and hook we publish should be signed with our keys, held in a register anyone can check, as PKI everywhere argued. Sigstore logs signatures publicly and SLSA records provenance. Then a copy found anywhere can be checked against the source, where the review, signature and current version live.

limits.para: Prices are not set; £1 a page is an example. No policy is audited yet; reviews and signatures come next. Scanners miss things, as Cisco's says and ours showed. Copying stays free; the licences do not change. The second meter is the book's site, and both are small.

sources.para: A voice memo of 20 October 2026; Claude Code's plugin security page; the Cisco, Snyk, NVIDIA and Anthropic scanners and marketplaces; Red Hat, Docker and Sonatype; Sigstore and SLSA; and earlier articles on paying after the value, forks, hooks, skills and PKI.
